claim: Gli1+ cells contribute to the development of meniscus horns from 2 weeks of age.
source: Using a Gli1 reporter line, we found that Gli1+ cells contribute to the development of meniscus horns from 2 weeks of age.
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 1 using Gli1CreER Rosa26 lsl-tdTomato mice at various ages.

claim: In adult mice, Gli1+ cells resided at the superficial layer of meniscus.
source: In adult mice, Gli1+ cells resided at the superficial layer of meniscus and expressed known mesenchymal progenitor markers.
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence imaging and immunostaining in Figure 1 and Figure 2.

claim: Gli1+ cells expressed known mesenchymal progenitor markers.
source: In adult mice, Gli1+ cells resided at the superficial layer of meniscus and expressed known mesenchymal progenitor markers.
evidence: Shown by immunostaining for Sca1, Cd90, Cd200, PDGFRα, Cd248, and Prg4 in Figure 2A and flow cytometry in Figure 2B.

claim: Meniscal Gli1+ cells possessed high progenitor activities under the control of Hh signal in culture.
source: In culture, meniscal Gli1+ cells possessed high progenitor activities under the control of Hh signal.
evidence: Demonstrated by CFU-F assays, proliferation assays, migration assays, and differentiation assays in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

claim: Meniscus injury at the anterior horn induced a quick expansion of Gli1-lineage cells.
source: Meniscus injury at the anterior horn induced a quick expansion of Gli1-lineage cells.
evidence: Shown by fluorescence imaging and quantification in Figure 4 following meniscus transection surgery.

claim: Meniscal tissue healed slowly, leading to cartilage degeneration.
source: Normally, meniscal tissue healed slowly, leading to cartilage degeneration.
evidence: Demonstrated by repair scores over time in Figure 4D and cartilage degeneration shown in Figure 6.

claim: Ablation of Gli1+ cells hindered the meniscus repair process.
source: Ablation of Gli1+ cells further hindered this repair process.
evidence: Shown by cell ablation experiments using Gli1ER/Td/DTA mice in Figure 4I-L.

claim: Intra-articular injection of Gli1+ meniscal cells right after injury accelerated the bridging of the interrupted ends.
source: Strikingly, intra-articular injection of Gli1+ meniscal cells or an Hh agonist right after injury accelerated the bridging of the interrupted ends and attenuated signs of osteoarthritis.
evidence: Demonstrated by histology and repair scores in Figure 5A-D showing reconnection at 4 weeks post-injury.

claim: Intra-articular injection of an Hh agonist right after injury accelerated the bridging of the interrupted ends.
source: Strikingly, intra-articular injection of Gli1+ meniscal cells or an Hh agonist right after injury accelerated the bridging of the interrupted ends and attenuated signs of osteoarthritis.
evidence: Demonstrated by histology and repair scores in Figure 5E-H showing reconnection at 4 weeks post-injury with PMA treatment.

claim: Intra-articular injection of Gli1+ meniscal cells attenuated signs of osteoarthritis.
source: Strikingly, intra-articular injection of Gli1+ meniscal cells or an Hh agonist right after injury accelerated the bridging of the interrupted ends and attenuated signs of osteoarthritis.
evidence: Shown by reduced Mankin scores and preserved cartilage structure in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Intra-articular injection of an Hh agonist attenuated signs of osteoarthritis.
source: Strikingly, intra-articular injection of Gli1+ meniscal cells or an Hh agonist right after injury accelerated the bridging of the interrupted ends and attenuated signs of osteoarthritis.
evidence: Shown by reduced Mankin scores and preserved cartilage structure in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Meniscal tears are associated with a high risk of osteoarthritis.
source: Meniscal tears are associated with a high risk of osteoarthritis but currently have no disease-modifying therapies.
evidence: Cited from established clinical knowledge about meniscal injuries and OA progression.

claim: Meniscal tears currently have no disease-modifying therapies.
source: Meniscal tears are associated with a high risk of osteoarthritis but currently have no disease-modifying therapies.
evidence: Statement about current clinical practice and lack of effective treatments.

claim: Meniscal injuries are important early events in the initiation and later propagation of osteoarthritis.
source: Beyond the short-term pain, disability, time from desired activities including work, meniscal injuries are important early events in the initiation and later propagation of osteoarthritis (OA) (Lohmander et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lohmander et al., 2007.

claim: Surgical treatments for meniscal injuries, including partial meniscectomy, do not delay the natural history progression of OA or may actually accelerate it.
source: From a clinical therapeutic point of view, surgical treatments, including the maximally preserving partial meniscectomy, while improving immediate symptoms, do not delay the natural history progression of OA or may actually accelerate it.
evidence: Statement about clinical outcomes of current surgical interventions.

claim: The adult meniscus is predominantly avascular.
source: As the adult meniscus is predominantly avascular, true biologic healing with surgical repair remains a viable treatment for only a small portion of individuals typically with tears contained within the red vascular zone (Makris et al., 2011).
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge about meniscus vascularity, supported by citation to Makris et al., 2011.

claim: True biologic healing with surgical repair remains a viable treatment for only a small portion of individuals with tears contained within the red vascular zone.
source: As the adult meniscus is predominantly avascular, true biologic healing with surgical repair remains a viable treatment for only a small portion of individuals typically with tears contained within the red vascular zone (Makris et al., 2011).
evidence: Clinical observation supported by citation to Makris et al., 2011.

claim: Human and rabbit meniscus contain mesenchymal progenitors with multi-differentiation abilities.
source: Using enzymatic digestion and clonal expansion methods, previous studies have demonstrated that human and rabbit meniscus contain mesenchymal progenitors with multi-differentiation abilities (Gui et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2016; Segawa et al., 2009; Shen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The superficial layer of meniscus was proposed to harbor the progenitors.
source: Interestingly, the superficial layer of meniscus was proposed to harbor the progenitors.
evidence: Statement based on previous research findings.

claim: Cells growing out of mouse meniscus explant exhibit stem cell-like characteristics and are located in the superficial zone in vivo.
source: By collecting cells growing out of mouse meniscus explant, Gamer et al. showed that these cells exhibit stem cell-like characteristics and are located in the superficial zone in vivo (Gamer et al., 2017a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gamer et al., 2017a.

claim: During injury, progenitors on the meniscus surface migrate from vascularized red zone to non-vascularized white zone for repair.
source: During injury, it has been observed that progenitors on the meniscus surface migrate from vascularized red zone to non-vascularized white zone for repair (Seol et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Seol et al., 2017.

claim: Meniscus progenitor cells in culture express several common mesenchymal progenitor markers, such as CD44, Sca1, and CD90.
source: While these cells in culture express several common mesenchymal progenitor markers, such as CD44, Sca1, and CD90, their in vivo properties and regulatory signaling pathways are not known (Shen et al., 2014; Seol et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shen et al., 2014 and Seol et al., 2017.

claim: The in vivo properties and regulatory signaling pathways of meniscus progenitor cells are not known.
source: While these cells in culture express several common mesenchymal progenitor markers, such as CD44, Sca1, and CD90, their in vivo properties and regulatory signaling pathways are not known (Shen et al., 2014; Seol et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement about gaps in current knowledge.

claim: Hedgehog signaling is essential for embryonic development and tissue homeostasis.
source: Hedgehog (Hh) signaling is essential for embryonic development and tissue homeostasis.
evidence: Established knowledge about Hh signaling pathway.

claim: Hedgehog signaling is one of few fundamental pathways that maintain adult stem and progenitor cells in various organs.
source: It is one of few fundamental pathways that maintain adult stem and progenitor cells in various organs, such as brain, skin, bladder, teeth, and others (Petrova and Joyner, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Petrova and Joyner, 2014.

claim: Following injury, Hh signaling can trigger stem and other resident cells to participate in repair.
source: Following injury, Hh signaling can trigger stem and other resident cells to participate in repair, and therefore, Hh upregulation is viewed not only as a natural response to injury but also as a way to stimulate tissue repair by activating stem cells.
evidence: General knowledge about Hh signaling in tissue repair.

claim: Gli1 was recently recognized as a marker for bone marrow, periosteal, and periarticular mesenchymal progenitors.
source: Gli1, an integral effector protein of Hh pathway, was recently recognized as a marker for bone marrow, periosteal, and periarticular mesenchymal progenitors (Shi et al., 2017; Tong et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019), suggesting that Hh signaling is also functional in the skeleton for maintaining tissue-specific stem and progenitors.
evidence: Supported by citations to Shi et al., 2017; Tong et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019.

claim: At 1 week of age, Gli1+ cells were only observed in the periarticular layer of articular cartilage, but not in the meniscus and other joint tissues.
source: In line with our previous report (Tong et al., 2019), at 1 week of age, Gli1+ cells were only observed in the periarticular layer of articular cartilage, but not in the meniscus and other joint tissues (Figure 1Ca-c).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence imaging in Figure 1Ca-c and consistent with previous publication.

claim: Long term tracing did not detect any Td signal in the meniscus at 1 week of age, confirming that neonatal meniscus does not harbor Gli1+ cells.
source: Long term tracing also did not detect any Td signal in the meniscus, confirming that neonatal meniscus does not harbor Gli1+ cells (Figure 1Cd).
evidence: Shown by lineage tracing data in Figure 1Cd.

claim: At 2 weeks of age, most cells in the anterior horn of the meniscus, both medially and laterally, were Td+.
source: At 2 weeks of age, most cells in the anterior horn of the meniscus, both medially and laterally, were Td+ (Figure 1Ce-g).
evidence: Shown by fluorescence imaging in Figure 1Ce-g.

claim: Six weeks of tracing confirmed that the entire anterior horn, but not the posterior horn, is labeled by Td at 2 weeks of age.
source: Six weeks of tracing confirmed that the entire anterior horn, but not the posterior horn, is labeled by Td (Figure 1Ch).
evidence: Demonstrated by lineage tracing shown in Figure 1Ch.

claim: At 4 weeks of age, Gli1+ cells were concentrated in the superficial layer of the anterior horn.
source: At 4 weeks of age, Gli1+ cells were concentrated in the superficial layer of the anterior horn; 6 weeks later, most cells in both superficial and central portions of the anterior horn were labeled by Td (Figure 1Ci–l).
evidence: Shown by fluorescence imaging in Figure 1Ci-l.

claim: 1–8 weeks of age represents the rapid growing phase for the meniscus.
source: Quantification along the length of the meniscus over the time indicated that 1–8 weeks of age represents the rapid growing phase for the meniscus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by morphological analysis and perimeter quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ihh expression was greatly increased at 4 weeks of age and maintained at the elevated level at 8 weeks of age.
source: Interestingly, Ihh expression was greatly increased at 4 weeks of age and maintained at the elevated level at 8 weeks of age, while Dhh expression only showed a tendency to increase during the same time period.
evidence: Shown by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 1E.

claim: Dhh expression only showed a tendency to increase at 4-8 weeks of age.
source: Interestingly, Ihh expression was greatly increased at 4 weeks of age and maintained at the elevated level at 8 weeks of age, while Dhh expression only showed a tendency to increase during the same time period.
evidence: Shown by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 1E.

claim: Ptch1, Smo, Gli1, Gli2, and Hhip mRNA showed significant increases at 4 weeks of age compared to 1 week of age.
source: We also observed significance increases of Ptch1, Smo, Gli1, Gli2, and Hhip mRNA at 4 weeks of age compared to 1 week of age.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 1E.

claim: Most increases in Hh signaling components declined at 8 weeks of age.
source: Most increases declined at 8 weeks of age.
evidence: Shown by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 1E.

claim: Gli3 expression decreased at 8 weeks of age.
source: Meanwhile, Gli3 expression decreased at 8 weeks of age and Shh mRNA was not detected at all time points.
evidence: Shown by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 1E.

claim: Shh mRNA was not detected at all time points during postnatal meniscal development.
source: Meanwhile, Gli3 expression decreased at 8 weeks of age and Shh mRNA was not detected at all time points.
evidence: Shown by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 1E.

claim: Ihh is the major responsible ligand for enhanced Hh signaling during postnatal meniscal development.
source: Thus, our data validated the enhanced Hh signaling during postnatal meniscal development and pointed out Ihh as the major responsible ligand.
evidence: Inferred from the expression pattern data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Slow cycling cells are considered quiescent stem cells.
source: Slow cycling cells are considered quiescent stem cells (Moore and Lyle, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moore and Lyle, 2011.

claim: Gli1+ cells at P30 contain much more EdU+ cells than Gli1- cells.
source: Applying a label-retention method on neonatal mice (EdU injections at P3-6 and Tam injections at P25-29), we found that Gli1+ cells at P30 contain much more EdU+ cells than Gli1- cells (Figure 1F,G), indicating that meniscus stem cells are enriched in the Gli1+ cell population.
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU labeling and quantification in Figure 1F,G.

claim: Meniscus stem cells are enriched in the Gli1+ cell population.
source: Applying a label-retention method on neonatal mice (EdU injections at P3-6 and Tam injections at P25-29), we found that Gli1+ cells at P30 contain much more EdU+ cells than Gli1- cells (Figure 1F,G), indicating that meniscus stem cells are enriched in the Gli1+ cell population.
evidence: Inferred from EdU retention data in Figure 1F,G showing slow-cycling properties.

claim: When mice reached mature and late adult stages (24 and 48 weeks of age), Gli1 mostly marked the superficial layer of both anterior and posterior horn of the meniscus.
source: When mice reached mature and late adult stages (24 and 48 weeks of age, respectively), Gli1 mostly marked the superficial layer of both anterior and posterior horn of the meniscus (Figure 1H).
evidence: Shown by fluorescence imaging in Figure 1H.

claim: There is a drastic reduction of Gli1+ cells in aged mice compared to adolescent mice.
source: Quantification of cells along the surface of meniscal horns revealed a drastic reduction of Gli1+ cells in aged mice compared to adolescent mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gli1 labels the entheses between anteromedial, posteromedial, anterolateral, posterolateral meniscus and the tibial plateau or femur condyle.
source: We found that Gli1 labels these entheses between anteromedial, posteromedial, anterolateral, posterolateral meniscus and the tibial plateau or femur condyle (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Shown by fluorescence imaging in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Gli1 labels the osseous ligamentous junctions between the anterior cruciate ligament or posterior cruciate ligament and femur or tibia.
source: In addition, Gli1 also labeled the osseous ligamentous junctions between the anterior cruciate ligament or posterior cruciate ligament and femur or tibia (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: Shown by fluorescence imaging in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B,C.

claim: The existence of Gli1-labeled cells on the meniscus surface was confirmed by Gli1 immunostaining.
source: The existence of Gli1-labeled cells on the meniscus surface was confirmed by Gli1 immunostaining (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Gli1+ cells were located in the superficial layer, but not in the central part, of meniscus horn in the adult mini-pig.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B, Gli1+ cells were located in the superficial layer, but not in the central part, of meniscus horn in the adult mini-pig.
evidence: Shown by immunohistochemistry staining in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Gli1+ meniscus cells co-express Sca1, Cd90, Cd200, PDGFRα, Cd248, and Prg4 in the superficial layer of the meniscus.
source: Immunostaining of mesenchymal markers, such as Sca1, Cd90, Cd200, PDGFRα (Boxall and Jones, 2012), and Cd248 (Naylor et al., 2012; Bagley et al., 2009) revealed their co-staining with Td+ signal in the superficial layer of the meniscus (Figure 2Aa-e).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining in Figure 2Aa-e.

claim: Gli1+ cells are Prg4+.
source: We found that Gli1+ cells are also Prg4+ (Figure 2Af).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence staining in Figure 2Af.

claim: Gli1+ cells are only 2% of digested meniscus cells.
source: Flow cytometry revealed that Gli1+ cells are only 2% of digested meniscus cells and that they express mesenchymal progenitor markers Sca1, CD90, CD200, and PDGFRα at a higher level than Gli1- cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gli1+ cells express mesenchymal progenitor markers Sca1, CD90, CD200, and PDGFRα at a higher level than Gli1- cells.
source: Flow cytometry revealed that Gli1+ cells are only 2% of digested meniscus cells and that they express mesenchymal progenitor markers Sca1, CD90, CD200, and PDGFRα at a higher level than Gli1- cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry quantification in Figure 2B.

claim: 72.8% of CFU-Fs from meniscus cells were Td+.
source: Interestingly, 72.8% of CFU-Fs were Td+, suggesting that Gli1+ cells have a high clonogenic activity (Figure 2C).
evidence: Demonstrated by CFU-F assay in Figure 2C.

claim: Gli1+ cells have a high clonogenic activity.
source: Interestingly, 72.8% of CFU-Fs were Td+, suggesting that Gli1+ cells have a high clonogenic activity (Figure 2C).
evidence: Inferred from the high percentage of Td+ CFU-Fs shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Sorted Td+ cells proliferated faster than Td- cells.
source: While both Td+ and Td- cell can grow in culture, sorted Td+ cells proliferated faster (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B) and migrated quicker (Figure 2D,E) than Td- cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by cell counting assay in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Sorted Td+ cells migrated quicker than Td- cells.
source: While both Td+ and Td- cell can grow in culture, sorted Td+ cells proliferated faster (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B) and migrated quicker (Figure 2D,E) than Td- cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by scratch-wound assay in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Td+ meniscus cells differentiated better into osteoblasts, adipocytes, and chondrocytes than Td- cells.
source: In addition, Td+ meniscus cells differentiated better into osteoblasts, adipocytes, and chondrocytes than Td- cells as shown by staining (Figure 2F) and marker gene expression (Figure 2G).
evidence: Demonstrated by differentiation assays and staining in Figure 2F and qRT-PCR in Figure 2G.

claim: Gli1+ cells possess the properties of mesenchymal progenitors: self-renewal and multi-lineage differentiation.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrated that Gli1+ cells possess the properties of mesenchymal progenitors: self-renewal and multi-lineage differentiation.
evidence: Concluded from multiple in vitro assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: GANT-61 reduced Gli1 expression in meniscus progenitors.
source: In line with previous reports (Srivastava et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2013), GANT-61 reduced Gli1 expression in meniscus progenitors while PMA increased it (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 3A and consistent with previous publications.

claim: PMA increased Gli1 expression in meniscus progenitors.
source: In line with previous reports (Srivastava et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2013), GANT-61 reduced Gli1 expression in meniscus progenitors while PMA increased it (Figure 3A).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 3A and consistent with previous publications.

claim: GANT-61 reduces the number of meniscus cells in culture over time.
source: Cell counting revealed that GANT-61 reduces the number of meniscus cells in culture over time while PMA increases cell number (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by cell counting assay in Figure 3B.

claim: PMA increases meniscus cell number in culture over time.
source: Cell counting revealed that GANT-61 reduces the number of meniscus cells in culture over time while PMA increases cell number (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by cell counting assay in Figure 3B.

claim: Hh signaling promotes the migration of meniscus progenitors.
source: Similarly, scratch assay showed that Hh signaling promotes the migration of meniscus progenitors (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Demonstrated by scratch-wound assay in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Hh signaling has an important action in promoting proliferation and migration of meniscus progenitors.
source: Our data demonstrated an important action of Hh signaling in promoting proliferation and migration of meniscus progenitors.
evidence: Concluded from the effects of GANT-61 and PMA on cell proliferation and migration shown in Figure 3.

claim: At 1–2 weeks post-surgery, the two ends of the meniscus retracted toward the synovium and ligament.
source: At 1–2 weeks post-surgery, the two ends of the meniscus retracted toward the synovium and ligament, respectively (Figure 4Ca-c).
evidence: Shown by histology in Figure 4Ca-c.

claim: Meniscus injury was accompanied by massive synovial hyperplasia that wrapped around the ends of the meniscus.
source: This was accompanied by massive synovial hyperplasia that wrapped around the ends of the meniscus and likely stabilized them.
evidence: Observed in histology shown in Figure 4Ca-c.

claim: At 4 weeks post-injury, the synovium returned to relatively normal thickness and the two cut ends of the meniscus were aligned but not connected.
source: At 4 weeks, the synovium returned to relatively normal thickness and the two cut ends of the meniscus were aligned but not connected (Figure 4Cd).
evidence: Shown by histology in Figure 4Cd.

claim: The connection between the two ends of injured meniscus gradually moved toward re-establishment but never reached the normal level even after 3 months post-surgery.
source: Over time, the connection between the two ends gradually moved toward re-establishment but never reached the normal level even after 3 months post-surgery (Figure 4Ce, f).
evidence: Demonstrated by histology and repair scores in Figure 4Ce,f and Figure 4D.

claim: Meniscus heals slowly in this injury model.
source: The meniscus repair scores summarized this trend (Figure 4D), suggesting that meniscus heals slowly in this injury model.
evidence: Shown by repair score quantification over time in Figure 4D.

claim: Starting from 2 weeks post-injury, Td+ cells appeared at the synovial ends and ligamental ends of injured meniscus.
source: Strikingly, starting from 2 weeks post-injury, Td+ cells appeared at the synovial ends and ligamental ends of injured meniscus (Figure 4Cg-l).
evidence: Shown by fluorescence imaging in Figure 4Cg-l.

claim: The number of Td+ cells at injured meniscus ends peaked around 4 weeks post-injury.
source: Their number peaked around 4 weeks, and gradually declined thereafter (Figure 4Cj-l).
evidence: Shown by fluorescence imaging in Figure 4Cj-l.

claim: Total cell density and the percentage of Td+ cells at both ends were significantly increased after injury, particularly at the ligamental end.
source: Total cell density and the percentage of Td+ cells at both ends were significantly increased after injury, particularly at the ligamental end (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification in Figure 4E,F.

claim: The expression of Hh signaling components increased after meniscus injury.
source: qRT-PCR further demonstrated the increased expression of Hh signaling components after injury (Figure 4G).
evidence: Shown by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 4G.

claim: Dhh, but not Ihh, was highly induced after meniscus injury.
source: Interestingly, different from the development stage, Dhh, but not Ihh, was highly induced after injury, suggesting that Hh ligands play distinct roles in meniscal development and injury repair.
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis in Figure 4G.

claim: Hh ligands play distinct roles in meniscal development and injury repair.
source: Interestingly, different from the development stage, Dhh, but not Ihh, was highly induced after injury, suggesting that Hh ligands play distinct roles in meniscal development and injury repair.
evidence: Inferred from the differential expression patterns of Ihh and Dhh during development versus injury shown in Figure 1E and Figure 4G.

claim: Many Gli1+ cells and their progenies are proliferative at 2 weeks post meniscus surgery.
source: An EdU incorporation experiment confirmed that many Gli1+ cells and their progenies are proliferative at 2 weeks post surgery (Figure 4H).
evidence: Demonstrated by EdU labeling in Figure 4H.

claim: In old mice (52 weeks of age), the expansion of Td+ cells after injury was remarkably attenuated.
source: In old mice (52 weeks of age), this expansion of Td+ cells after injury was remarkably attenuated and the end-to-end reconnection was much less with a lower repair score than young adult mice 4 weeks later (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), indicating that aging diminishes the repair ability of meniscus.
evidence: Shown by fluorescence imaging and repair scores in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Aging diminishes the repair ability of meniscus.
source: In old mice (52 weeks of age), this expansion of Td+ cells after injury was remarkably attenuated and the end-to-end reconnection was much less with a lower repair score than young adult mice 4 weeks later (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), indicating that aging diminishes the repair ability of meniscus.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced Td+ cell expansion and lower repair scores in aged mice shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Td+ cells in meniscus were drastically decreased by 54.5% one day after Tam injections in Gli1ER/Td/DTA mice.
source: One day after the Tam injections, Td+ cells in meniscus were drastically decreased by 54.5%, as shown by both sagittal and coronal views of meniscus horns (Figure 4J).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence imaging and quantification in Figure 4I,J.

claim: Three months after injury, while two meniscus ends loosely reconnected in vehicle-treated mice, those in Tam-treated Gli1ER/Td/DTA mice were still well separated.
source: Three months later, while two meniscus ends loosely reconnected in vehicle-treated mice, those in Tam-treated mice were still well separated, leading to a significant reduction of repair score (Figure 4K,L).
evidence: Shown by histology and repair scores in Figure 4K,L.

claim: Gli1-lineage cells are essential for meniscal healing.
source: These data clearly indicate an essential role of Gli1-lineage cells in meniscal healing.
evidence: Concluded from the cell ablation experiment showing impaired repair in Figure 4I-L.

claim: Healthy human meniscus did not show Gli1 staining.
source: Healthy meniscus did not show Gli1 staining (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown by immunohistochemistry in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In moderate and severe degenerated human meniscus, Gli1 was readily detectable in cell clusters characterized by Ki67+ staining.
source: However, in moderate and severe degenerated meniscus, Gli1 was readily detectable in cell clusters formed in various sizes and characterized by Ki67+ staining, indicating that Gli1+ cells are proliferative.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunohistochemistry in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gli1+ cells are proliferative in degenerated human meniscus.
source: However, in moderate and severe degenerated meniscus, Gli1 was readily detectable in cell clusters formed in various sizes and characterized by Ki67+ staining, indicating that Gli1+ cells are proliferative.
evidence: Inferred from Ki67 co-staining with Gli1 in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is an expansion of Gli1+ cells in human meniscus tissues during degeneration.
source: These results confirmed an expansion of Gli1+ cells in human meniscus tissues and a potential action of Hh signaling in human meniscus repair.
evidence: Concluded from the presence of Gli1+ cell clusters in degenerated human meniscus shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A single injection of Gli1+ cells right after injury resulted in a reconnection of the synovial and ligamental ends of injured meniscus at 4 weeks.
source: Strikingly, a single injection of cells right after injury resulted in a reconnection of the synovial and ligamental ends of injured meniscus at 4 weeks, leading to a repair score of 4.8 (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by histology and repair scores in Figure 5B,C.

claim: At 4 weeks post-injury, the two meniscus ends were well separated in both vehicle and Gli1- meniscus cell-treated groups, with a repair score of only 1.8 and 1.9, respectively.
source: At the same time, these two meniscus ends were well separated in both vehicle and Gli1- meniscus cell-treated groups, with a repair score of only 1.8 and 1.9, respectively.
evidence: Shown by histology and repair scores in Figure 5B,C.

claim: In Gli1+ cell-treated mice, collagen fibers crossed the broken ends of the meniscus.
source: However, in Gli1+ cell-treated mice, collagen fibers crossed the broken ends of the meniscus, suggesting that the repair does occur at the structural level.
evidence: Shown by polarizing images in Figure 5B.

claim: Injected Gli1+ cells expand and contribute to the newly formed connection at the injury site.
source: Fluorescence imaging revealed that injected Gli1+ cells expand and contribute to the newly formed connection at the injury site (Figure 5D).
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence imaging in Figure 5D.

claim: Four weeks after PMA treatment, the injured ends of meniscus were reconnected based on gross morphology, safranin O/fast green staining, and imaging of collagen fibers.
source: Four weeks later, the injured ends of PMA-treated meniscus were reconnected based on gross morphology, safranin O/fast green staining, and imaging of collagen fibers (Figure 5F), leading to a repair score of 4.9 (Figure 5G).
evidence: Demonstrated by histology and polarizing images in Figure 5F and repair scores in Figure 5G.

claim: There were more Td+ meniscus cells in PMA-treated joints than vehicle-treated joints at 1 week after injury.
source: There were more Td+ meniscus cells in PMA-treated joints than vehicle-treated joints at 1 week after injury (Figure 5H).
evidence: Shown by fluorescence imaging in Figure 5H.

claim: Hh agonist does not affect overall joint calcification.
source: MicroCT scanning of mouse joints detected no change in the calcified meniscus volume and a trend of decrease in osteophyte volume at 3 months post surgery and pur treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Hh agonist does not affect overall joint calcification.
evidence: Demonstrated by microCT analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activating Hh signaling has a therapeutic effect on meniscus repair.
source: These data clearly indicated a therapeutic effect of activating Hh signaling.
evidence: Concluded from the improved repair with Gli1+ cell injection and PMA treatment shown in Figure 5.

claim: The meniscus injury model caused cartilage degeneration at 2 months post injury.
source: Similar to the surgical destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) model of OA, our meniscus injury model caused cartilage degeneration, such as partially loss of proteoglycan, surface fibrillation, and reduction in uncalcified cartilage thickness at 2 months post injury (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by histology and quantification in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The calcified cartilage layer was not eroded at 2 months post meniscus injury, suggesting a moderate OA.
source: Meanwhile, the calcified cartilage layer was not eroded (Figure 6B), suggesting a moderate OA with a Mankin Score of 6.9 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Shown by histology and Mankin scoring in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Injections of either Gli1+ cells or PMA greatly reduced cartilage degeneration.
source: Strikingly, injections of either Gli1+ cells or PMA greatly reduced cartilage degeneration by retaining proteoglycan content, cartilage surface smoothness, and the structure of uncalcified cartilage.
evidence: Demonstrated by histology in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Gli1+ cell treatment led to a reduction in Mankin Score by 35%.
source: These treatments led to a reduction in Mankin Score by 35% and 53%, respectively.
evidence: Shown by Mankin score quantification in Figure 6C.

claim: PMA treatment led to a reduction in Mankin Score by 53%.
source: These treatments led to a reduction in Mankin Score by 35% and 53%, respectively.
evidence: Shown by Mankin score quantification in Figure 6C.

claim: OA knees show reduced paw withdraw threshold compared to sham knees.
source: Using this assay, we observed that OA knees show reduced paw withdraw threshold compared to sham knees.
evidence: Demonstrated by von Frey assay in Figure 6D.

claim: OA-related pain was mostly attenuated in Gli1+ cell- or PMA-treated knees.
source: However, this OA-related pain was mostly attenuated in Gli1+ cell- or PMA-treated knees (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by von Frey assay in Figure 6D.

claim: A similar level of cartilage degeneration was observed in control and PMA-treated mice 2 months after DMM surgery.
source: Two months later, we observed a similar level of cartilage degeneration in control and treated mice (Figure 6E,F), suggesting that the effect of Hh signaling on OA development is mediated through meniscus repair but not through directly acting on cartilage.
evidence: Shown by histology and Mankin scores in Figure 6E,F.

claim: The effect of Hh signaling on OA development is mediated through meniscus repair but not through directly acting on cartilage.
source: Two months later, we observed a similar level of cartilage degeneration in control and treated mice (Figure 6E,F), suggesting that the effect of Hh signaling on OA development is mediated through meniscus repair but not through directly acting on cartilage.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of PMA on cartilage in DMM model shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: Gli1+ cells are a major subset of meniscal mesenchymal progenitors.
source: In this work, by using a lineage tracing mouse line, cell culture, and a meniscus injury model, we demonstrated that Gli1+ cells are a major subset of meniscal mesenchymal progenitors and that those Hh-responsive cells are critical for meniscus development and injury response.
evidence: Concluded from multiple experiments including lineage tracing, in vitro characterization, and injury studies shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: Hh-responsive cells are critical for meniscus development and injury response.
source: In this work, by using a lineage tracing mouse line, cell culture, and a meniscus injury model, we demonstrated that Gli1+ cells are a major subset of meniscal mesenchymal progenitors and that those Hh-responsive cells are critical for meniscus development and injury response.
evidence: Concluded from lineage tracing during development, injury-induced expansion, and ablation studies shown in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: Aging reduces the Gli1+ progenitor population in healthy meniscus.
source: Moreover, aging reduces this Gli1+ progenitor population in healthy meniscus as well as their expansion after injury, which is consistent with attenuated healing in old mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and injury response in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Aging reduces the expansion of Gli1+ cells after injury.
source: Moreover, aging reduces this Gli1+ progenitor population in healthy meniscus as well as their expansion after injury, which is consistent with attenuated healing in old mice.
evidence: Shown by reduced Td+ cell expansion in aged mice after injury in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The activation of Hh/Gli1 signaling in adult meniscus leads to accelerated meniscus healing process.
source: On the therapeutic side, the activation of Hh/Gli1 signaling in adult meniscus leads to accelerated meniscus healing process and the delay of OA changes, indicating a protective role of Hh signaling on meniscus against degeneration.
evidence: Demonstrated by Gli1+ cell injection and PMA treatment experiments in Figure 5.

claim: The activation of Hh/Gli1 signaling in adult meniscus leads to the delay of OA changes.
source: On the therapeutic side, the activation of Hh/Gli1 signaling in adult meniscus leads to accelerated meniscus healing process and the delay of OA changes, indicating a protective role of Hh signaling on meniscus against degeneration.
evidence: Demonstrated by reduced cartilage degeneration in treated mice shown in Figure 6.

claim: Hh signaling has a protective role on meniscus against degeneration.
source: On the therapeutic side, the activation of Hh/Gli1 signaling in adult meniscus leads to accelerated meniscus healing process and the delay of OA changes, indicating a protective role of Hh signaling on meniscus against degeneration.
evidence: Inferred from the therapeutic effects of Hh activation shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Gli1+ cells do not contribute to the early development of meniscus.
source: Surprisingly, Gli1+ cells do not contribute to the early development of meniscus.
evidence: Shown by absence of Td+ cells at 1 week of age in Figure 1Ca-d.

claim: There must be other distinct progenitor population(s) contributing to meniscus development besides Gli1+ cells.
source: Since menisci undergo rapid growth postnatally and Gli1+ cells are absent from the meniscus body, our data indicated that there must be other distinct progenitor population(s) contributing to meniscus development.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of Gli1+ cells in meniscus body and the rapid growth of meniscus shown in Figure 1.

claim: Gli1- meniscus cells are able to proliferate and differentiate in vitro albeit with less activities compared to Gli1+ cells.
source: Indeed, we found that Gli1- meniscus cells are also able to proliferate and differentiate in vitro albeit with less activities compared to Gli1+ cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro assays comparing Gli1+ and Gli1- cells in Figure 2.

claim: Gli1+ cells rarely contribute to the inner cells of meniscus at the adult stage probably due to the low turnover of meniscus tissue.
source: At the adult stage, we found that Gli1+ cells are mainly located at the superficial layer of meniscal horns. They rarely contribute to the inner cells of meniscus probably due to the low turnover of meniscus tissue.
evidence: Inferred from lineage tracing data showing Gli1+ cells restricted to superficial layer in adult mice in Figure 1.

claim: Gli1+ cells play an important role in meniscus tissue regeneration.
source: However, similar to their counterparts in the periosteum (Shi et al., 2017) and tendon enthesis (Schwartz et al., 2015), they play an important role in tissue regeneration.
evidence: Demonstrated by injury-induced expansion and ablation studies in Figure 4, and supported by citations to similar findings in other tissues.

claim: The meniscus injury model established by transection of the anterior horn is suitable to study the beneficial effects of Hh signaling on meniscus repair and meniscus damage-related OA progression.
source: Hence, our model is suitable to study the beneficial effects of Hh signaling on meniscus repair and meniscus damage-related OA progression.
evidence: Inferred from the characteristics of the injury model showing slow repair and OA development described in Figure 4 and Figure 6.

claim: Synovial Gli1+ cells may also contribute to meniscus regeneration.
source: Notably, we also observed a quick expansion of synovium enriched with Gli1-lineage cells at the early stage of repair. Therefore, we cannot exclude the possibility that synovial Gli1+ cells also contribute to meniscus regeneration.
evidence: Observed in histology showing synovial hyperplasia with Td+ cells in Figure 4.

claim: Endogenous Gli1+ meniscus cells are likely responsible for meniscus repair.
source: That being said, our data showed that Gli1+ primary meniscus cells injected into knee joints incorporate into meniscus tissue and accelerate repair, indicating that the endogenous Gli1+ meniscus cells are likely responsible for the repair.
evidence: Inferred from cell transplantation experiments showing incorporation and repair in Figure 5D.

claim: It is possible that fibrochondrocytes in the deep layer of meniscus produce the Hh signals.
source: Since Ihh from the prehypertrophic chondrocytes is known for regulating long bone development through endochondral ossification (Olsen et al., 2000), it is possible that fibrochondrocytes in the deep layer of meniscus produce the Hh signals.
evidence: Speculated based on analogy to Ihh production in cartilage, supported by citation to Olsen et al., 2000.

claim: Rodents have bony ossicles in the meniscus horns.
source: However, rodents are different from human by having bony ossicles in the meniscus horns (Shaw and Martin, 1962).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shaw and Martin, 1962.

claim: Porcine meniscus has similar anatomic distribution of Gli1+ cells as mouse meniscus.
source: To show the clinical relevance of our research, we first demonstrated that porcine meniscus has similar anatomic distribution of Gli1+ cells, suggesting a conservation of this patterning between species.
evidence: Shown by Gli1 immunostaining in mini-pig meniscus in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: There is a conservation of Gli1+ cell patterning in meniscus between species.
source: To show the clinical relevance of our research, we first demonstrated that porcine meniscus has similar anatomic distribution of Gli1+ cells, suggesting a conservation of this patterning between species.
evidence: Inferred from similar Gli1+ cell distribution in mouse and pig meniscus shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The work identified a novel progenitor population in meniscus.
source: Taken together, our work identified a novel progenitor population in meniscus and proposes a new treatment for repairing injured meniscus and preventing osteoarthritis.
evidence: Concluded from the comprehensive characterization of Gli1+ cells throughout the manuscript.

claim: The work proposes a new treatment for repairing injured meniscus and preventing osteoarthritis.
source: Taken together, our work identified a novel progenitor population in meniscus and proposes a new treatment for repairing injured meniscus and preventing osteoarthritis.
evidence: Based on the therapeutic effects of Gli1+ cell injection and PMA treatment shown in Figures 5 and 6.
